content: Integrating specific interventions into existing intrapartum and immediate postpartum care packages can effectively promote behavioral changes among healthcare providers. For example, the use of tools such as patient records and registers can support this process. Various strategies to address barriers and facilitate implementation are outlined in Section 4.2 of the guidelines. The implementation and impact of these recommendations will be monitored at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. In collaboration with the monitoring and evaluation teams of the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research and the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, data on the implementation of these recommendations at country and regional levels will be collected and evaluated in the short to medium term. This evaluation will assess their impact on national policies in individual WHO Member States. Methods such as interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based audits may be used to gather relevant data on the use of interventions outlined in the guidelines. For postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) prevention, WHO recommends using the coverage of prophylactic uterotonics as a process indicator. This indicator is calculated as the number of women receiving prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labor divided by the total number of women giving birth. Additionally, assessing the use of specific uterotonics may be necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the quality of care related to PPH prevention and treatment. WHO has developed specific guidance for evaluating the quality of care for severe maternal complications, including PPH, using near-miss and criterion-based clinical audit concepts. Monitoring the quality of uterotonic drugs available in low-resource settings can help guide skilled health personnel in selecting the most effective uterotonic options for PPH prevention in their specific contexts. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) convenes regularly to review WHO’s portfolio of maternal and perinatal health recommendations. This group helps prioritize new and existing questions for recommendation development and updates. These recommendations will be reviewed and prioritized by the GSG. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendations will be updated. If no new reports or information are identified, the recommendations may be revalidated. Any concerns about the validity of a recommendation will be promptly communicated via the WHO Department for Reproductive Health and Research website, and plans will be made to update the recommendation as needed. WHO also welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates of these recommendations.
